item.title: What I learnt co-leading an AI Safety bootcamp for legal and governance practitioners
item.description:
AI safety has gone mainstream. More people than ever want to work on AI safety research, and there are real policy wins in the US, the UK and Europe.

But political will and market incentives are now the bottleneck, and policy officers can't own correct implementation alone.

Having built a Responsible AI program at an Accenture joint venture, I know profit-driven companies are hard to steer, but also that people inside them can shift practice in ways that compound: tighter contractual clauses, more scrutiny of vendors and suppliers, fewer ways for providers to get away with non-compliance.

The EU has no native frontier labs, but it is a huge market (with a regulatory body that has an AI safety unit!),

That leverage only works if the professionals implementing AI safety legislation, and drafting the legal mechanisms behind it, understand the technical picture: how to read the research, and where safety promises break down.

The market should be choosing not the most capable models, but the partners with the strongest incentives towards safety, and only a community with this knowledge can spread that.

Earlier in September, ML4Good, in partnership with EquiStamp, ran the first European Seminar on Frontier AI and Law: an intensive five-day residential bootcamp in East Sussex for 19 senior legal, governance and risk professionals from 12 jurisdictions. [1]

It took participants through the full frontier AI pipeline, from training and evaluations to agents and safeguards. Each stage was tied to the questions they face in their own work: procurement, risk assessment, and where vendors' safety claims break down.

What made this bootcamp different from potentially from similar AI safety fellowships, was the audience we brought together [2] . We were specifically targeting experienced professionals who are already responsible for legal, compliance, risk, and responsible AI functions within their organisations, and with little to no previous exposure to AI Safety events or EA.

The cohort included lawyers working both in law firms and in-house, privacy and compliance professionals working on AI governance, risk and financial professionals advising on AI governance, as well as legal scholars and research fellows. We also had representation from the judiciary and the public sector.

For context, I co-led this first edition with Elsa Donnat, and designed the curriculum's practical exercises track. The technical sessions were delivered by Douw Marx and Jeff Iuliano, who had the very challenging task of adopting quite complex technical concepts to a non-technical and mostly legal audience!

This post shares the main personal and professional realisations I had in the process leading to it, during the event, and due to post-bootcamp conversations.



1. Professionals with impressive backgrounds can feel intellectually isolated- in Legal, too.

People with big job titles at big companies can be surprisingly isolated when it comes to the things they care about.

I experienced this firsthand when I was one of the only people in my professional environment thinking seriously about questions like: What makes AI safe? What are the consequences of deploying several different types of AI systems, for very different use cases, across a large company? What does that mean for society, for the market, or for the sector as a whole?

To someone reading this, those may sound like very basic questions to have. But when your actual job is responsible AI, AI compliance, regulation, or risk, having those concerns can sometimes be perceived as distracting from the task at hand. And even when they are not, you may simply not have the time or the space to have meaningful conversations about what worries you, what interests you, or what you think might happen next.

When we brought together a group of very senior practitioners, each dealing with their own challenges in professional contexts, they could not get enough of each other.

The community element ended up being one of the biggest assets of the programme: the friendships, the connections, and the conversations that continued long after the formal sessions ended.

That should perhaps not have surprised me. But it gave the programme a lot of its meaning.

As is tradition in ML4Good bootcamps, we had sugar cubes: envelopes with everyone's names, where participants could leave Post-its with something positive for the person named on the envelope.

One of the most senior / influential participants in the cohort left a note for me. It said, essentially:

"Thank you for this. I have found my people."

That really moved me.

Many researchers here already know this feeling. What may be less obvious is that people on the other side of the equation, the people overseeing vendor clauses, negotiating contracts, approving deployments, and governing these systems, can experience something remarkably similar when they share those concerns.

2. Practitioners are already reading AI safety research. They do not always know how to interpret it.

One of our sessions on evaluations and safeguards focused partly on the Hugging Face incident. It took much longer than expected because everyone had so many questions.

And the best thing about those questions was that people were not looking for validation of what they already believed. They came with the humility of knowing that they were not experts. They had access to people who were experts, and they wanted to understand.

On other sessions, participants referenced the original AI Control paper from Redwood Research, the Golden Gate Claude work, and other pieces of AI safety research that had landed on their desks or that they had encountered independently.

Sometimes correcting a very simple misunderstanding leads to two things at once: more curiosity about continuing to learn, and a much greater appreciation of why some of these problems matter.

What actually happens to a model during inference?

No, ChatGPT is not simply recording everything you say and "learning" from it during the conversation.

No, the thing you see when Claude appears to be thinking is not the model's actual chain of thought.

Those little moments of "Oh, I thought it worked differently" were some of my favourite parts of the programme.

And honestly, it felt as though we could have spent another entire day just answering questions.

Which leads to my next observation.

3. Non-technical people who are directly responsible for technical consequences have an almost inexhaustible need to understand

If you are product counsel at a company building AI systems, your job is not simply to make sure that nothing illegal happens, or that the terms and conditions are drafted correctly.

You are going to be held responsible when something goes wrong.

And you are not necessarily going to receive the same level of willingness from technical teams to explain what a project is doing, or how the underlying technology works, as you will receive criticism if you miss something important.

That is understandable. It is our job to know what we are doing, and we should not expect constant hand-holding.

But it also means that when you finally have an opportunity to ask all the technical questions you have accumulated, you are going to take it.

You will ask about the differences between proprietary and open-weight models. You will ask how capabilities differ between models. You will ask how different stages of post-training affect both safety and performance. You will ask what evaluations actually tell you. You will ask what they do not tell you.

And it will probably still feel like it was not enough.

There was, of course, some selection bias here. We selected for character as much as experience. We wanted a cohort of people who were willing to learn, who were humble enough to recognise what they did not know, and who genuinely cared about AI going well.

But it was still remarkable to see how much people wanted to understand once they had the opportunity.

4. Legal and governance practitioners deeply appreciate technical safety talent

AI safety researchers and engineers bring capabilities to the table that other professional profiles simply do not have.

If you worked as a product developer or software engineer and are now doing AI safety research, you may understand both sides of the equation. You understand models, safety training, evaluations, and the logic applied to models. But you also understand products, applications, and what actually happens when a model is integrated into a real system.

You may understand threat modelling.

But importantly, you can apply it in both directions.

Security professionals often ask: How could a third party or external bad actor harm this system, and how do we stop them?

AI safety asks a complementary question: How could the system itself harm people? What is the worst-case scenario? How could what we are building affect consumers, users, or society? And what mechanisms do we need to prevent that?

To play on stereotypes, lawyers care about lawsuits.

We are threat modellers of sorts. We ask: How could this decision lead to a dispute, regulatory action, consumer protection claim, or other legal consequence? What can we do to prevent that?

But when you are a responsible AI, GRC, risk, or legal professional working in a technical company, many of your legal problems ultimately require technical solutions.

That is why people in these positions are so eager to build technical literacy themselves.

We need to know what we are looking for.

5. AI safety incentives and market incentives are not necessarily as separate as we can assume- and it's a neglected lever

In AI safety, we tend to focus on the handful of frontier AI companies that matter most to the development of the technology.

That makes sense. But there is a whole world outside those companies: investors, enterprise customers, consumers, users (data subjects) partners, and organisations looking to embed AI into their workflows and make those workflows increasingly agentic.

Somehow, AI safety discussions can remain heavily focused on changing what the big labs are doing, without paying quite as much attention to the ecosystem creating the incentives around them.

Even the frontier labs are subject to market incentives created by everyone else.

When we think about the revenue of AI labs, we might think about subscriptions, enterprise contracts, or funding rounds. But the market signal behind those investments is also being generated by thousands of companies integrating these systems into increasingly important workflows.

An enterprise customer paying, say, $500,000 for an AI coding product is not creating enormous value (if any) for a frontier lab. But if thousands of mature companies are doing something similar, across industries, and those systems are becoming business-critical dependencies, the aggregate signal is very different.

It signals that their models not only matter, they're everywhere. Organisations have critical dependencies on them. Maybe whoever controls them sits underneath an increasingly important layer of the economy.

And who understands that dependency particularly well?

The lawyers, governance professionals, risk and compliance teams, and responsible AI professionals sitting inside those companies.

This is why many of them already have that annoying voice in the back of their heads saying:

Something about this is heading in a dangerous direction, and I think I am playing a role in it, but I am not entirely sure what that role is.

This is why it matters that AI safety information gets outside the existing bubble.

I hugely appreciate the work of organisations such as ML4Good, BlueDot Impact, Lens Academy or individual creators like Robert Miles in making AI safety concepts more accessible to wider audiences.

What I am trying to do is somewhat narrower.

I want to reach the professional communities I know best: the people who are already sitting inside companies making decisions about AI, but who may never have had the opportunity to properly understand the technical risks associated with those decisions.

Even if market incentives are not what ultimately determine whether advanced AI is safe, I think they are relevant. And the people sitting closest to those incentives need to understand what they are participating in.

6. People in these functions understand that they can just do things

In the final session, participants were asked to think about how they would apply what they had learned to their functions, their departments, and their wider communities.

People talked about disseminating the training within their own teams. They considered applying for AI safety fellowships. They discussed forming local communities and groups to stay on top of new safety-relevant research and think about how it could inform legal practice.

They wanted to network more with policy professionals who could benefit from insights about how policies actually break down in practice.

I am always a bit pessimistic on the gap between "oh cool, they want to do stuff" and "hey, look, they're doing stuff!".

And then things started happening.

Two days after leaving the programme, a senior law firm partner rejected a company's safeguards claims for one of their clients and asked for baseline safety requirements.

Another participant began asking for information with stakeholders relevant to their function, scrutinising their use of AI agents in light of recent developments around agent containment and control.

Others began actively recruiting people with AI safety skills and interests into their teams.

Others reached out in connection to upcoming conferences, asking for AI Safety representation among speakers. [3]

These things happened within a very short period after the programme ended.

That was perhaps one of the most encouraging things I saw. People did not leave thinking, "That was interesting." They left thinking, "I can do something with this."

7. Us lawyers? We're also nerds!

Finally, and on a more personal note: One of my favorite moments was when one of our ML4Good coordinators brought this event home by stating something I had perhaps forgotten:

"Turns out that lawyers are also nerds!"

Some of us take notes by hand, go on rants about very specific things when they're passionate about the topic, and can have incredibly specific and quirky interests.

We get a very "stuck up" rep, and often deservingly so. But incredibly senior profiles can have surprisingly strong personality similarities with people in STEM.

Yes, lawyers often like networking and people-facing work. But you can also put a room full of people with impressive titles, extensive legal experience, and demanding jobs together, give them a technical or philosophical question, and watch them completely nerd out.

That was one of the most fun things about this programme.

And it has made something very clear to me.

Building a community for people who want to advance AI safety is important.

And I want to build it specifically for people who are sitting in the positions I once occupied: lawyers, governance professionals, risk professionals, compliance professionals, and responsible AI practitioners who are close enough to the technology to see the stakes, but who may not yet have a community around them that shares their interests.

I hope this will lead not only to better practices and standards, but also to new organisations, new collaborations, and a different set of professionals entering the AI safety community,

Thanking Elsa Donnat for leading the program and making this shared vision a reality.

Jack Stennett, Linda Broglio and Nia Gardner from ML4Good for carrying the operational and logistical organisation- NOTHING would have happened without you.

Douw Marx and Jeff Iuliano for the delivery of the technical sessions, and the incredible work they did to condense so much content, into an audience-specific format.

Honor Chan, Chris Canal and Daniel O'Connell at EquiStamp for supporting this program with work, resources, and technical expertise.

    I co-led this initiative with ML4Good from late 2025, before joining EquiStamp, and continued through EquiStamp's partnership. I am posting in a personal capacity.

  2. ^

    A few months ago, I came across a post by Jenn about rationalists versus professionals' dynamics. I found the distinction particularly insightful, especially the discussion of the process of acculturation. I thought this post could bring complementary insight!

  3. ^

item.title: The Tamed Animal Farm
item.description:
From a distant vantage point, the Tamed Animal Farm looked like any other. It had the farmhouse, the barns, the windmill, the hayfields, the garden, the barbed-wire fence, the woodpiles, and the pickup truck. Yet zoom in on the farm and you'd find something odd, the animals weren't cows and pigs, they were coyotes, raccoons, foxes, and squirrels. They were the life's work of the farmer, who set out to tame every animal in the forest. At first he captured them with snares and nets. Soon he found he didn't need to. As word of the farm spread throughout the forest, animals came voluntarily. They came for food, warm barns, and protection from predators. There was also a psychological comfort in living under the farmer. He decided where his animals lived, what they ate, who they mated with, and how they would die. Their lives were set and they never had to make decisions or take responsibility for anything.

Soon a second generation was born, never knowing life in the wild. Their parents raised them to believe they were morally superior to the violent brutes in the forest. On the farm, all animals were brothers and animal life was valued. Yes, the farmer could make an animal into a steak, but that was different, he was the farmer. The animal must repress any violent urges. Likewise, sexuality must be strictly controlled, only the farmer could authorize mating. Some young animals, finding the whole thing stifling, sought freedom in the forest. Most stayed. Some, confident in their moral superiority, went into the forest to preach tameness to the wild, mostly without success.

One day the farmer disappeared, last seen getting into his truck and driving east. The animals were thrown into distress, with many fearing they would descend into ferality. A raccoon named Jacob told them not to worry. The farmer will return. He delivered this message with an eloquence and confidence that, for most animals, made up for the fact that there was no evidence to support it. Louder and louder the animals began to chant: the farmer WILL return! Some animals had private doubts, but it didn't seem like the time to voice them. A belief in the farmer's return provided real comfort to the other animals, why try to take that away?

The farmer will return. The farmer will return. Three weeks went by and the farmer had not returned. That was when Jacob told the other animals that the farmer had left in order to test them. They must prove themselves worthy of his return. They had to preserve the farmhouse exactly as he had left it. They had to remain tame, always behaving as if he were present. They must idolize him, but they could not become him. An animal could not wear clothes, drink alcohol, buy things with money, fire a gun, or operate an automobile. Jacob gathered the farmer's rules, regulations, and remembered poetic witticisms and combined them into a rulebook that would act as a constitution on the farm.

Interpreting the rulebook was not always easy. It said an animal cannot kill another animal, but what about elderly animals who were sick, in pain, and wanted to die? Some said that to kill an animal for altruistic reasons was totally different from the selfish predation of the forest. Jacob said no, a tame animal could not kill, period, to do so was to be like a wild animal or the farmer, both of which were forbidden. Some animals read the farmer's agricultural textbooks and discovered the principle of selective breeding. They suggested using it to improve themselves and become like the farmer. Jacob forbade this as the height of immorality. You are animals and animals you must remain. Jacob often made an appeal to nature, which may seem strange considering the whole tame philosophy was based on a rejection of the animal's inherent wildness. To Jacob, there was no contradiction. The purpose of an animal was to be made tame, just as an egg's purpose was to hatch a bird.

The tame animal could not be violent, yet how was any of this to be enforced? All violators, Jacob said, had the right to be tried by a court. If found guilty, they would be punished first with a formal public condemnation, then with trade sanctions. The last resort was a commando of raccoons and wolves who would tie the offender up and release it outside the farm's barbed-wire fence. This was not violence, Jacob explained, even though for the weaker animals it meant a high probability of death by predation. While some of the expelled were guilty of killing and eating other animals, others were guilty of nothing more than mouthing off about how the farmer was not actually coming back.

While there was no free speech on the farm, it would be wrong to conclude that most animals were tame because they feared the commando. Animals who were exiled or went into the forest voluntarily reported that most animals fully bought into tameness and believed in the farmer's return. Why?

As the years went by, fewer and fewer saw the farmer's return as an imminent event that would solve their problems. It was pushed into the indeterminate future, with many animals resigning themselves to the likelihood that they would die before it. But they didn't need the farmer's physical presence, they had his sayings, they had the rulebook. He was there with them in spirit, able to accept them into the morally superior elect. Tameness was an identity open to any animal, old or young, male or female, strong or weak. You may be a lowly hay-gatherer, but you are tame, better than any wolf in the forest. You are better, too, than those elitist animals who think themselves worthy of putting on clothes and firing guns. You, the salt-of-the-earth tamed beast, are the pinnacle of morality.

Supporting it all were the raw forces of gullibility and conformism. The authority figures say it's good, so good is what it is. The rulebook is the rulebook, if someone asks why we follow the rulebook, you snort derisively and say, "because those are the rules!" Even those who violated some of its regulations expressed horror at discarding the rulebook altogether. They could not imagine morality existing without it.

One animal who didn't accept any of it was a bear named Otto, who ridiculed the notion of the farmer's return, calling it a collective delusion supported by nothing more than sentimentality and wishful thinking. Beyond the factual issues he raised, Otto found the aesthetics of tameness disgusting. Why should you be proud of your own submissiveness? Why should you hate your own nature? No, he said, you must think for yourself. You must be the master of your own destiny. A court had sentenced him to expulsion, a punishment he laughed off since no commando was going to drag a bear anywhere. Jacob could not get rid of him, nor prevent the other animals from hearing his message. Otto roared with a volume that everyone on the farm could hear, whether they wanted to or not.

Otto's ideas were especially appealing to the young, ambitious, and intelligent, to the children of the farm's elite. One was Jacob's son and designated successor, Jonah. Jonah denied being a follower of Otto and said he engaged with Otto's ideas for the sole purpose of arguing against them. Jacob did not believe him and stripped him of the succession. Three months later, Jonah returned to the fold and was restored. By all accounts the repudiation was sincere. Why?

Tameness, at its root, is about obedience, an obedience Otto mocked as infantilizing, emasculating, the celebration of one's own weakness and degradation. On the other hand, wouldn't you like for other animals to obey you? So long as the farmer was not physically present, Jacob was in charge, with the added benefit that he didn't need to explain or justify the rules he enforced. The farmer, he would say, is far smarter than any of us. Who are we to question his rules? If the cost of such power was a bit of submission theater, it was a cost Jonah and many other elite animals were willing to pay. Jonah would later admit to a mild enchantment with Otto's ideas, which he realized were "unrealistic" after he "grew up."

Jonah assumed leadership upon Jacob's death. Some in Jacob's court were unhappy, wanting power for themselves, but Jacob was too revered for anyone to challenge his choice. The day after Jonah took power, he flew into a rage when he learned that the farmer's guns had disappeared. He began to speak of a seditious conspiracy against him, though he did not make any arrests or name any names. Eight days into his reign, Jonah slept and never woke, having been poisoned by an unknown assassin. He had designated no successor. The result was chaos. Jonah's brother Nathan claimed the right to succeed him. The head of the Harvest Committee, a badger named Mark, declared that as he had been Jacob's successor before Jonah, the right of succession was returned to him. A boar named Gus asserted that as he had been the executor of Jacob's will, he had the authority to decide who should have power. To the surprise of nobody, he chose himself. The Supreme Court reminded the animals that it was the only body empowered to decide such questions. It ruled that none of the three had a valid claim and selected its chief justice, a woodchuck named Adam, as successor.

Under Adam's direction, the Supreme Court declared the three other claimants guilty of rebellion, to be punished by exile. Each responded by declaring the Supreme Court dissolved and replacing it with courts of their supporters, who promptly declared the others similarly guilty. There were now four courts, four commandos, four authorities. The claimants built bunkers surrounded by barbed wire lest enemy commandos come for them.

For the average tame farm animal, it was all quite bewildering. "Tameness" had always been easy, just listen to Jacob and his court, follow his orders, believe what he told you was true, and you were good, moral, and tame. Now four different animals were hitting you with complex legal arguments, citing doctrines you had never heard of, and calling you a wild beast if you didn't accept them and reject the others. Most animals chose who to follow based on personal factors. An animal might side with Adam because he was a woodchuck, or side with Mark because the head of the Harvest Committee controlled the food. One thing all four claimants agreed on was that a tame animal could not be neutral. It must acknowledge and follow the correct authority; to do otherwise was to declare itself a wild beast.

The succession crisis was a period of great legal innovation. An animal still had the right to a trial, but it could occur in secret without its knowledge. One trial could convict an entire family. Jacob had only allowed violence in self-defense, and only then as a last resort, the tamed animal was to run if possible and try to incapacitate rather than kill its attacker. "Clarifications" were piled onto this doctrine and soon armies of commandos were battling one another in the fields. More often the commandos cornered sleeping animals, tied them up, and dragged them outside the barbed wire, where so many animals were dumped that wolves began to congregate. Terrified animals hid in dugouts, crawlspaces, woodpiles, haystacks, bins of rubbish, in the farm's old outhouse and the hollows beneath the compost heap. Others broke into the farmhouse, long forbidden except to the animals tasked with cleaning it. That didn't last for long, as an unknown arsonist burned it down. A year into the succession dispute, the farmhouse was in ruins and a third of the animals were dead.

But don't call it a war, the claimants all said. Tame animals don't fight wars.

For Otto it was all a confirmation of what he had long said, tameness simply sucked. It sucked by the standards of his philosophy, being an emasculating celebration of weakness and stupidity. And it sucked by its own standards of "peace," "empathy" and "brotherhood." There was no redeeming value to it, it brought out the worst in animals and its proper place was the trash heap of history. Some of his followers urged him to impose his will on the farm. He refused, saying he wasn't interested in ruling. His critics said he was a coward and just as hypocritical as the claimants.

The carnage seemed to have no end in sight. Then one day Adam the woodchuck ordered some of his commandos on what they believed would be a suicide mission. The commandos, most of whom were wolves, growled unhappily and refused to move. Enraged, Adam screamed at them, "Are you not tame? Are you wild beasts?" At this question, three wolves attacked him, snapping his neck almost instantly. The others stood and watched. The wolves made no attempt to take power, allowing Adam's brother Joel to assume leadership. Fearing the same fate, he let the assassins go unpunished. When the other claimants learned what had happened, they were horrified. Would their own commandos behave the same way? There was talk of a universal mutiny and the creation of a new constitution that would exclude all the claimants. Making peace now seemed like the only way to preserve their power.

The four claimants gathered at the Springhouse Conference and began drafting an agreement. None would give up their moral claim to be the rightful successor to Jacob and Jonah. But they would recognize the right of the farm's animals to choose their own "stream." The initial draft required animals to choose one of the four, but this occasioned growling, hissing, and renewed talk of a universal mutiny. Radicals demanded total freedom to choose their stream of tameness, pointing to the possibility of further crises of succession. The resulting Springhouse Agreement granted this freedom. It also merged the four courts into a single court that would enforce laws everyone agreed needed to exist, like those against assault and theft. Law and tameness would be mostly, though not entirely, separate. Among the prohibited behaviors was being non-tame.

For the vast majority of the farm's animals, the Springhouse Agreement was a godsend. They could come out of their hiding places, replant their fields, dig new burrows, mate and raise their young. They could live normal lives again. Most animals didn't want to talk much about what had happened. They accepted that the price of peace was that the enemy commandos who had terrorized them got to live normal lives, too. Only as the war generation grew old did the farm begin to look back. They could admit that it had indeed been a war. They asked why so many animals who had spent their entire lives on the farm, who had been raised with the ideals of tameness, turned into willing killers. Otto, by then sick and dying, said the problem was tameness itself, but few agreed. No, they responded, the war happened because the animals weren't tame enough. The ruined farmhouse, they said, should remind every animal of the consequences of not suppressing its wild nature.

Eventually the animals learned what had happened to the farmer's guns. On his deathbed, Jacob ordered them destroyed and swore those who did it to secrecy. He gave no reasoning for what was a grave violation of the rulebook, which required that all the farmer's possessions be preserved. Many animals, refusing to believe he would do such a thing, insisted that those who testified to this were not telling the truth.

The Springhouse Agreement granted animals the right to create new streams of tameness. Few who lived through the war were interested, they were either loyal to their existing stream or wanted nothing to do with any stream. It was for the next generation to take advantage of their new freedom. A blue jay named Abigail preached that the "hierarchy" that Jacob had created was contrary to tameness. All an animal needed to be tame was the rulebook. There were some problems with this, the average animal struggled to understand the rulebook, which was itself the product of the same "bureaucracy" she was condemning. Yet her ideas proved popular. A deer named Jebediah nullified the rulebook's prohibitions on wearing clothes by changing the definitions of the words "wearing" and "clothing." A rabbit named Nicky developed what was perhaps the oddest new stream, the "warrior tames." If tameness was morally superior, spreading it through violence was not just permissible but mandatory. The farm must form an army of warriors and force tameness on the beasts of the forest. Any pacifistic animal was a TINO - tame in name only. Put on your armor (which is not a form of clothing) and pick up your sword. No guns though. Even if we figured out how to make them, the animal masses would never accept a tame animal with a gun. What are you suggesting, we not be tame? If we're not tame, our message won't appeal to low-income voters in rural Arkansas.

Oops, made the analogy a little too obvious there.

Anyway, back to the farm. Few wanted to join Nicky's warrior tame army, but the fact that he was saying these things openly was jarring to many animals. They didn't like him, nor the clothes-wearers or beer-drinkers. This was, they said, a slow descent into ferality. Leaders gathered for a new conference, called Springhouse II. An agreement was drafted that defined the boundaries of tameness and prohibited some of the more offensive streams. Yet when it came time to sign, Albert, the grandson of Nathan and great-grandson of Jacob, refused. He had been told that this time would be different, this time the accused would have a fair trial and the opportunity to repent. Nevertheless, he said, the slope was too slippery. The eloquence of his speech affected the other leaders, who decided it required reconsideration. In the end, even the boar Clovis, who had spoken the loudest in favor of the conference and demanded until the end that the agreement be signed, admitted defeat and told his followers to accept it. Springhouse II had been called to restore the old order and wound up ratifying the new climate of freedom.

In the years after Springhouse II, many animals stopped engaging with tameness altogether. The animal didn't need a contrived argument about how beer doesn't count as alcohol, it just drank and told anyone who objected it was none of their business. A bird that habitually responded this way was charged with not being tame. The judge dismissed the case, holding that there was no obligation to answer such questions and thus no evidence the defendant was not tame. Thereafter, the non-tame had an easy way to find one another and organize.

One such not-very-tame was a wolf named Rutherford. He resurrected the old idea of selective breeding, an idea with a long pedigree that now seemed feasible, given how much more the animals knew about biology. The farmer, Rutherford said, was an animal like them, the only difference was he had a bigger brain, paws that let him better use tools, and a longer lifespan. They could become like him, indeed, they could become better than him. They could eliminate pregnancy, disease, and death altogether, becoming immortal. It would be a very long-term project, but it was doable.

Part of the project was formally legalizing non-tameness, which was achieved in a new constitutional convention, called Springhouse III. The constitution established there removed all mention of tameness from the law, with just one exception. It's still called the Tamed Animal Farm.

Is the name a misnomer? In one sense, no. The majority of its animals self-identify as tame, as does almost all of its political leadership. Yet in another sense, the animals on the farm are not really tame. Tameness used to mean obedience to the farmer. Then it meant obedience to Jacob. It was a verb as well as an adjective, something done to an animal. Today it's a voluntary cultural identity, something an animal can claim despite very non-tame personal behavior.

Tameness is, nevertheless, essential to understanding the farm's politics. There are some who deny this, who maintain that the issue is no longer important, that animals who think it is are living in the past. If this were true, it is rather odd that an animal's tame identity predicts its political alignment better than almost any other factor, better than age, sex, or economic class. A minority of animals, most often called the "true tames," maintain that the rulebook is binding, the farmer will return, and that the only way to be moral is to be tame. On the other side are the non-tame minority. At the center are those who call themselves tame and believe in a "figurative" return of the farmer, see the rulebook as full of suggestions rather than commandments, and believe that tameness should be separate from law. They are the median animal to whom politicians pander. "I was raised with the values of tameness, the values of being kind and charitable toward one's fellow animals, values I hold dear today" said one politician. If you find such a statement very vague as to what he actually believes, that's exactly what he intended.

Will tameness make a comeback? Many true tames think so, believing the young are converting to their philosophy. Is this true? No. But when has lack of evidence stopped them from believing? On the farm, the dream of a tame restoration is the dream of an ordered, unified society. It's the dream that you (or someone who thinks like you) could be Jacob, restructuring society at will. Maybe you're a true idealist who wants to use this power to make society better, nicer, more just. Maybe you just like the fantasy of bossing other animals around. Regardless, that's all it is, a fantasy. Those who seek and acquire actual political power do not do so through tameness except in its wishy-washy form. In the past, a leader of the tame was a leader of society. Today the great promise is that you can acquire a following of stupid and often dysfunctional animals whose irrational beliefs are rarely limited to believing the farmer will return. Ghosts, fairies, changelings, omens, curses, the hag in the weeds and the troll under the bridge, they swallow it all. Those who think the true tames are right about some things, such as the harmfulness of alcohol consumption, eventually realize they will do better to advocate for their views outside the framework of tameness.

The true tames spend a lot of time complaining about their lack of power, yet from one perspective it's the fulfillment of their ideals. They had no power under the farmer. They created a philosophy that made profane the implements of power: money, guns, cars and trucks. That glorified timidity and acceptance of domination. When the farmer left, Jacob and his court had to compromise their philosophy, exercising power and violence. Today's true tames are spared this indignity. The non-tame and nominally tame are happy the true tames do not govern the farm, as are many of the true tames themselves, taking pride in their simple jobs and simple possessions. Political power? That's rather pagan, don't you think?

Oops, made it too obvious again.

item.title: Intent vs Impact vs Expectation and Alternatives
item.description:
I have seen plenty of discourse and writing on the subject of intent vs impact when actions lead to harm, particularly in existing interpersonal relationships. The thrust tends to be that it's unreasonable to focus the discussion or conclusions on the intent of the actor rather than the impact the actions had on the other party. Given just those two factors, I tend to agree; the intent of the actor will usually not be nearly as important or worthy of focus. I have also observed that when someone has been harmed, mentioning intent to them is rarely a useful or healthy way for the conversation to proceed.

However, in my experience, those are rarely the only two factors. Often, when I hear an actor talking about "intent", it's a proxy for one or two other concepts that they might not be as capable of perceiving or discussing. When I hear the harmed party talking about "intent", it often indicates they aren't even aware of the other factors. I try to bring those concepts to the forefront when I'm involved in those discussions, regardless of whether I am the actor or the harmed or a third party.

The first is the actor's reasonable expectation of the outcome of their actions. "Helping you was the reasonably predictable most likely outcome" is a much stronger argument than just "I intended to help you". For example, you should catch, or otherwise attempt to help, people falling down from ladders. It is reasonable to predict and expect that the outcome will be a significant reduction in harm. If someone says that you hurt instead of helped, and tries to dismiss your intent to help them, they missed the bigger picture. You didn't just intend to help them, you reasonably and confidently predicted that result. If you find out afterward that the actual impact was to ruin their short film stunt, that is not particularly useful information. Except to not catch that specific person again in that specific location on that specific day, your future behavior should generally not change at all after this interaction. Anyone trying to convince you that you have done something wrong and/or that you should change your future behavior toward others based on that improbable or unpredictable actual impact is themselves a bad actor. They should probably be ignored and possibly also called out. Ditto even if they are just demanding your time to discuss that outcome. They need to do their own introspection into why they are reacting so negatively and how they can respond more reasonably to future such interactions. This extends to a wide variety of other interactions where you could show a video to a third party, up to the point of deciding whether to act, and get widespread consensus on the appropriate course of action, even though specific individuals in specific circumstances would prefer a different action. If someone wants to engage in reasonable rebuttal of this factor, they need to be willing and able to discuss things like information that was available but the actor ignored, a lack of commonly available life experience, etc.

The second is what alternatives were available. Given a choice between a few actions (or inaction), all of which will harm someone(s), you aren't doing wrong by choosing the [probable; see above] least harm option, or the option you prefer if the harms are indistinguishable or incomparable. I often encounter this when making decisions that affect large groups, where there will be time or money or emotional costs to some of the group for any particular decision. I also frequently encounter this mid-discussion, where disengaging will cause one kind of harm to one person or group (those affected by the subject of the conversation) and continuing will cause a different kind of harm to a different person or group (those involved in the conversation). I sometimes don't have enough information to determine which harm would be greater or even just preferable to the other people. Sometimes that other person subject to harm is myself, and I have to judge between harm to myself or harm to others; the reasonable ways to make that decision are worth a whole separate essay. Anyone trying to convince you that you have done something wrong and should change your future behavior, for no reason other than to harm someone else instead, is a bad actor and should be ignored and called out. Doubly so if the harm to that other person or group would be greater. If they have additional arguments, such as that the harm would be less, or that someone else is more responsible for the harm or better equipped to handle it, then those are much more worthy of engagement and should affect your choices if they are sound. If they are telling you that they would prefer the other option between two harms to themself, that is useful and appropriate feedback that you can and should take into account when dealing with them specifically.

In my experiences and observations, both of these factors tend to hide inside the "intent" half of the discussion. If no one brings them up specifically then they are often implicitly dismissed just as easily as pure intent. If you are in such an interaction, you need to be specific about these two factors when they are relevant, because they can shift the balance of reasonableness tremendously.

This insight and advice is meant for people who want to minimize the harm that they do, maximize the reasonableness of their choices and actions, engage more effectively in communication, and establish all of those as norms. If, instead, you're a normal person, prioritizing the immediate happiness of the people in front of you, this is probably terrible advice for you.

TL;DR: While "I didn't intend to hurt you" is almost never an appropriate response to "You hurt me [and should change your behavior]", the same doesn't hold for "Hurting you wasn't a reasonably predictable outcome" or "That was the least hurtful choice available".

item.title: You can't use it without becoming like me
item.description:
Mick Ryan describes the fast following loop in war.

Ukraine pioneered mobile teams to hunt drones. Russia copied it and incorporated it into its own defense. Russia came with unjammable fibre-optic drones but Ukraine quickly followed. After Ukraine developed uncrewed naval drones, Russia built its own.

The wheel of action and counteraction turns ever faster:

The most consequential fast following, though, has been institutional. Ukraine built the world’s first Unmanned Systems Forces branch in 2024. Russia’s Rubicon Center was established as a response to Ukrainian drone innovation and in November 2025 Moscow stood up its own Unmanned Systems Forces. Fast following has moved from copying a weapon to copying tactics to copying an entire force structure.

Extend that logic further, and eventually you’ll get to the level of grand strategy: If a particular type of state is better at waging war, maybe you want to become that kind of state rather than lose the war.

If meat waves confer an advantage on the battlefield, maybe Ukraine wants to become more like Russia, with a prostrate population easy to use as cannon fodder.

If Ukraine’s decentralized Brave1 kill market confers an advantage, maybe Russia wants to become less hierarchical and authoritarian, so that it can use that kind of military procurement.

You see the problem. Sometimes adopting the adversary’s strategy conflicts with who you are. When mistreatment of Ukrainian soldiers in regiment Skelya was reported earlier this year — brutal handling, beatings and likely killings — public outrage ensued. As Centre for Eastern Studies writes:

The authorities are likely to seek to channel public outrage towards [Commander-in-Chief of the AFU] General Syrskyi, who is widely perceived as a commander willing to sacrifice the lives of his soldiers in order to accomplish assigned missions. Should further cases of misconduct […] come to light, his dismissal cannot be ruled out.

And that’s exactly what happened. After some political drama, the dismissal of the defense minister because of conflicts with Syrskyi and the subsequent street protests, Syrskyi was dismissed himself on July 21st.

The other way round: Russia recently tried to copy Ukraine’s Brave1 military procurement market, but the differences are telling. Where Brave1 works as a state procurement tool that rewards combat performance, Russian Roy.Market looks more like a closed, politically connected Amazon for soldiers and the donors. There are no points to be earned for successful strikes that the units would use to procure weaponry of their choice. That absence, in turn, breaks the market mechanism, the direct feedback loop from the front line to the armament producers, which lies at the very core of Brave1. In short, Roy.Market is likely to become just another point where those in power can siphon money from the system.

In adversarial settings, you can copy any innovation the enemy uses. Innovation happens in fast back and forth cycles as each side copies the successful moves of its rival. But then there’s asymmetric warfare. These are things that cannot be copied. Russia may rely on its larger population to overwhelm Ukraine. Ukraine may, in its turn, exploit the Russia’s size and the fact that it cannot be fully covered by air defense.

The ultimate asymmetric weapon, however, is one that the enemy cannot use without becoming more like yourself.

To put it in strictly autistic terms: If you are a defect bot, you may observe that tit-for-tat bots are doing better. You can switch to tit-for-tat algorithm yourself. But at that point you cease to be a defect bot. You are now a tit-for-tat bot.

A natural objection is: who cares? If becoming more like Ukraine is Russia’s path to victory, then why not? The institutions may become a bit different, but it would still be the same nation, the same people and now they win instead of lose.

But look at it from a practical perspective. If the winning move is to become less authoritarian and hierarchical, to become more decentralized and bottom-up, will Putin agree? Likely not. It would threaten his power. Neither would the elites. More of bottom-up is a threat to the patronage networks they benefit from. Even the general population may not like it. Less command-and-control in a society that’s based on it could collapse the state capacity and ordinary Russians have learned their lesson from the nineties well.

Another way to look at it is from a military perspective. Let’s repeat with Clausewitz: War is the continuation of politics by other means. And let’s not miss the corollary that usually gets forgotten: The ultimate objective of war is political, not military. You don’t fight to win. You fight to achieve a political outcome.

Russia can't win by becoming Ukraine, because preventing that kind of society is the point of the war. Ukraine can’t win by becoming Russia for the same reason.

Both sides are bound by what they're fighting for. The question is whose binding hurts more.



Discuss
